rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]
rows.description: She explains the cause, apologises once, and presents a week-by-week plan with a named owner and twice-weekly updates. The client can now judge the recovery rather than only the problem.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: accountability partner, delegation, mental simulation

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.description: The messenger explains that the infrastructure team caused the issue. The client hears excuses and asks who is accountable on the vendor side, which weakens confidence in both teams.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: delegation, mental simulation

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the call and adjusting communication cadence [Revision]
rows.description: After the call the team notes the client wanted more frequent updates. They switch from weekly emails to short Monday and Thursday notes, and the relationship steadies.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: accountability partner, delegation, mental simulation

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: delegating the message to the person with the relationship [Thinking]
rows.description: Realising the client trusts the delivery head most, the account lead asks him to join and lead the discussion. The personal bond helps the client stay open to the recovery plan.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: accountability partner, mental simulation

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: listening separately to each side first [Action]
rows.description: A lead meets two colleagues one at a time, asking what happened and what each needs. Both feel heard, and she learns the fight began over unclear ownership of a release task.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, root cause analysis

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: Asking why repeatedly, the lead finds the quarrel is not about personality. Overlapping task assignments and a missing handover note keep creating blame between the two.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: clarifying roles and shared working rules [Action]
rows.description: She writes a simple responsibility list, agrees a handover format, and asks both to confirm it. The rule replaces argument about who should have done what.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, root cause analysis

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: facilitated joint conversation with agreed ground rules [Action]
rows.description: The lead brings both together with rules: one speaks at a time, focus on the work, and end with one request each. They leave with two agreed changes to try for two weeks.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, root cause analysis

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: hoping it fades without intervention [Pitfall]
rows.description: Wanting to avoid awkwardness, the lead ignores sharp comments in meetings. The tension spreads, others pick sides, and one member starts looking for another job.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: root cause analysis

rows.subtopic: A conflict between two team members
rows.subtype: Approach: taking sides with the senior performer [Pitfall]
rows.description: The lead trusts the more experienced colleague and asks the other to adjust. The junior feels dismissed and goes quiet, while the real ownership gap remains unresolved.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, root cause analysis
